questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x{e}^{xy}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,0,-1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,0)}(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =(-1)y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Given that the point $P(1,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot 1\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4})(x-1) \\ z-0 & =1(x-1) \\ z & =x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{\pi }{4} \\ z=x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x-1$ (or $x-z+-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-1⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩$ is also parallel to it.

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Given that the point $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=-\frac{2{x}^{2}+y}{{y}^{3}}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(\sqrt{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(\sqrt{2},2) & =-\frac{2(\sqrt{2})^{2}+2}{{2}^{3}} \\  & =-\frac{4+2}{8} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}(y-2) \\ z-\frac{1}{2} & =-\frac{3}{4}(y-2) \\ z & =-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=\sqrt{2} \\ z=-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P(2,\frac{1}{2},1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+\frac{1}{y}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(2,\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2}) & =2+2(2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2})+\frac{1}{(1/2)} \\  & =2+4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(2,\frac{1}{2}) & ={f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2})(y-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =4(y-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =4y-2 \\ z & =4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,\frac{1}{2},1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2 \\ z=4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=4y-1$ (or $4y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,4,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,4,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+4\,k \\  & =⟨0,1,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,4⟩.$

The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(\frac{\pi }{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1) \\  & =2\cdot 1-0 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(\frac{\pi }{2},1) & ={f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1)(y-1) \\ z-0 & =2(y-1) \\ z & =2y-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z=2y-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=2y-2$ (or $2y-z-2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,2,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,2,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+2\,k \\  & =⟨0,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,2⟩.$
